articles.title: Hisense Infinite Matt Glass : que vaut la plaque à induction en verre mat à 749 € ?
articles.text:
| Commodité d'emploi |  | 
| Nombre de foyers | 4 | 
| Diamètre du plus grand foyer | 19.5 cm | 
| Foyers jumelables | Les deux | 
| Boosters | 4 | 
| Minuteurs | individuel | 
| Niveaux de puissance | 9 | 
| Options | connexion à une hotte aspirant, capteur de température, stop & go | 
Plus que par sa puissance de 7360 W, la plaque de cuisson par induction Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass se démarque de la concurrence en raison de son revêtement mat, mais aussi de ses programmes de cuisson automatiques.
Le verre mat sur les plaques de cuisson gagne peu à peu du terrain. Depuis l'Electrolux Saphir Matt Série 700 de 2024, ce revêtement séduit de plus en plus les utilisateurs, qui y voient un matériau plus simple à entretenir que le verre brillant, mais aussi plus résistant aux traces de doigts et petits incidents du quotidien, au premier rang desquels les rayures.
Hisense avait déjà utilisé le verre mat sur la HI63218SR et reconduit l'expérience sur la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass, plus sophistiquée. En effet, ce modèle d'une puissance totale de 7360 W, paramétrable sur neuf paliers, possède aussi une sélection de programmes automatiques pour faciliter la vie en cuisine et gérer quatre foyers. À ce sujet, précisons que les paires de droite et gauche peuvent être jumelées pour former deux surfaces de cuisson de grande superficie.
Pourvue d'un système de communication entre la plaque et une hotte compatible pour que la puissance de l'une s'adapte à la puissance de l'autre (technologie Hob To Hood), la plaque HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass peut aussi s'appairer à un smartphone doté de l'app ConnectLife, tout cela pour un ticket d'entrée s'élevant à 749 €.
Nous l'avons dit, le petit monde des plaques de cuisson a subi une lame de fond dernièrement avec l'arrivée des revêtements mats. La Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass n'échappe pas à la règle et abandonne la brillance du verre pour un noir mat assez réussi. La surface est ornée de sérigraphies blanches pour aider à placer les ustensiles. Hisense a choisi un ensemble de lignes, de pointillés et de tout petits repères pour aider l'utilisateur à positionner ses casseroles. Et ne tournons pas autour du pot, ce n'est clairement pas la méthode la plus pratique ; les cercles restent les indications les plus claires.
En allumant la Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass, le bandeau de commandes s'illumine dans une belle couleur ambrée. Contrairement à l'immense majorité des plaques de cuisson, ce n'est pas un afficheur électronique à segments qui indique la puissance utilisée, mais une diode sous un chiffre soigneusement calligraphié. Vous l'aurez deviné, on modifie la puissance en appuyant sur le chiffre décidé ou en faisant glisser son doigt sur la suite de caractères. Attention, il faudra parfois de bons yeux pour bien distinguer le niveau choisi. En revanche, on apprécie que chaque inducteur bénéficie de son propre slider. Ainsi gagne-t-on en réactivité puisqu'il n'est pas nécessaire de sélectionner la zone à paramétrer, de faire les modifications et de recommencer pour un autre foyer.
Ces réglages en accès direct ne sont pas valables pour la minuterie. En effet, si on peut mettre sur pied un compte à rebours pour l'ensemble de la plaque, on peut aussi paramétrer une durée de cuisson pour un inducteur, mais il faudra toucher l'icône d'horloge près de la réglette de l'inducteur concerné, puis modifier les réglages via les flèches qui vont s'allumer au centre du panneau de commandes. On s'y fait assez vite et cette option ne demande pas autant de réactivité que les modifications de puissance.
Les chefs les plus tatillons pourront peut-être se sentir bridés par le faible nombre de paliers de puissance de la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass, quand certaines plaques de notre comparatif (la Bosch PIX63SHC1F par exemple) proposent plus de 15 niveaux. Cependant, dans le cadre d'une utilisation quotidienne, cela ne devrait pas être trop gênant.
L'une des caractéristiques de la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass est l'intégration de six modes de chauffe automatique : maintien au chaud, faire fondre, mijoter, griller, frire et porter à ébullition. Les plus anglophobes devront céder à la langue de Harry Kane puisque les noms sont inscrits en anglais (keep warm, stir, fry... and so on and so forth), mais avec un peu de mémoire, on maîtrise le tout. Pour passer de l'un à l'autre, il suffit d'effleurer la touche A. Le nom de la fonction (in english) va s'afficher et la plaque se réglera d'office sur la puissance requise : a piece of cake… ou plutôt simple comme bonjour.
Hisense insiste énormément sur la reconnaissance automatique des ustensiles. Même si celle de la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass est, il est vrai, particulièrement rapide, cette fonctionnalité n'a rien d'inédit.
La plaque de cuisson Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass peut être appairée à un smartphone équipé de l'app ConnectLife. La connexion entre les deux produits ne pose pas vraiment de difficulté, mais les opportunités offertes sont très limitées. Le fabricant a prévu le téléchargement de recettes, un planificateur de repas, la création de recettes avec l'IA ou encore un manuel d'utilisation numérique. On pourra aussi programmer sa plaque à distance, mais sans lancer la cuisson — celle-ci ne démarrera qu'en appuyant sur une touche de la plaque. Ce n'est clairement pas pour ses fonctions connectées que l'on choisira la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass.
Depuis la HI63218SR, Hisense n'a pas eu le temps de faire des progrès concernant les performances de cuisson. Celles de la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass ne resteront donc pas dans les annales, mais devraient suffire pour le commun des mortels.
Avant toute chose, signalons que les quatre zones de cuisson de la HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass sont absolument similaires : même taille, même puissance. En découle un manque de polyvalence puisqu'on ne pourra pas privilégier un petit feu pour réduire doucement une sauce ou un énorme foyer pour cuire le plat de pâtes familial du mercredi midi.
Et c'est d'autant plus dommage que la plaque Infinite Matt Glass gère mal les basses puissances. En effet, après 2 h de fonctionnement à la puissance la plus faible, la température dans notre bain d'huile atteint 80 °C, très loin du résultat idéal de 55 °C, la température à laquelle le chocolat est le plus facile à travailler pour les pâtissiers.
La HI63218SR ne brille pas non plus par sa rapidité de montée en température. Il lui faut 6 min très précisément pour que 3 l d'eau passent de 25 °C à 95 °C. Pour que le liquide atteigne 100 °C, 30 s supplémentaires de patience sont requises.
En raison de leur taille, les inducteurs fournissent une chaleur homogène au sein des ustensiles. Les patates sautées devraient donc toutes être cuites de la même façon sans avoir à trop les remuer.
Cependant, comme toujours, en utilisant les zones jumelables, il faudra s'attendre à des disparités de température notables. On réservera donc leur utilisation à un plat en sauce qui peut mijoter longtemps et on évitera la poissonnière qui risque de livrer une truite trop cuite au niveau de la tête et de la queue, mais pas assez au niveau du corps.
Attention, nous avons remarqué que la plaque fonctionnait par intermittence pour simuler les paliers de puissance intermédiaires. Cela ne devrait pas avoir d'incidence sur la cuisine de tous les jours, mais mieux vaut le savoir.
La puissance maximale que nous avons pu atteindre avec la Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass est de 7410 W. Grâce à cela, on peut activer les quatre foyers à la puissance maximale, mais pas en mode booster.
La HI6443SRWF se montre plutôt sobre en énergie. Pour arriver au terme de notre test de montée en température (pour rappel, faire passer 3 l d'eau de 25 °C à 100 °C en utilisant le mode boost), elle n'a besoin que de 0,34 kWh. Certes, la Bosch Série 6 PIX63SHC1F reste toujours la plus sobre dans ce domaine (0,29 kWh seulement), mais les résultats obtenus par Hisense sur cette épreuve sont très bons.
Les plaques de cuisson par induction sont des produits plutôt discrets et la HI6443SRWF InfiniteMattGlass ne fait pas exception à la règle. À mi-puissance, notre sonomètre atteint 41 dB (A) pour grimper jusqu'à 51 dB (A) quand on enclenche le mode boost. Pas de quoi casser les oreilles !
La plaque de cuisson Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass est pétrie de qualités. On citera notamment des réglages de puissance en accès direct ou les différents modes de cuisson automatiques proposés, qui aideront les novices de la cuisson par induction à maîtriser leur nouvel équipement. C'est pourquoi on regrette tant que Hisense ait choisi de l'équiper de quatre inducteurs parfaitement identiques, ce qui a pour conséquence de limiter sa polyvalence. Autre effet indésirable, on ne pourra pas recommander ce modèle, pourtant peu gourmand en énergie, aux cuisiniers exigeants, tant la maîtrise des basses puissances est insatisfaisante.
La concurrence est rude sur le marché de la plaque à cuisson à induction, et il est très difficile de se distinguer. La Hisense HI6443SRWF Infinite Matt Glass est un peu chère par rapport à des modèles plus performants comme l'Electrolux Série 600 FlexiBridge EIV64453, qui elle aussi embarque deux zones jumelables. Pour ceux qui souhaitent plus de polyvalence, la Bosch Série 6 PIX63SHC1F reste un excellent choix, tout comme la Hisense HI63218SR Infinite Matt Glass (200 € moins coûteuse, tout de même) pour les amateurs de revêtement mat.

articles.title: Temporal 5x’d AI spend and doubled revenue. CEO Samar Abbas says he can’t prove they’re connected.
articles.text:
Temporal 5x’d AI spend and doubled revenue. CEO Samar Abbas says he can’t prove they’re connected.
Temporal co-founder and CEO Samar Abbas is guiding the company’s adoption of AI tools across engineering and business workflows. (Credit: The New Stack photo illustration)
For the final two weeks of the year, Temporal clears its calendars. The company calls it a reading period: no meetings, just time to explore, learn, and build. Over the ‘25 holidays, co-founder and CTO Maxim Fateev spent his time with coding agents. He came back describing work that once took six months, now done in less than thirty days, according to the company. Co-founder and CEO Samar Abbas credits that break with setting the company’s AI posture for the year. A fellow co-founder returning with numbers like that, he says, is a stronger argument than any company directive.
That shift, from a veteran engineer to a veteran engineer with Claude Code, led Abbas toward redirecting the company’s efforts. Temporal sells durable execution, the failure-resistant plumbing that keeps long-running software alive through crashes and outages, and it sells it to companies that cannot afford downtime. Nvidia and Netflix are among the companies using its workflow technology.
In February, the company raised $300 million at a $5 billion valuation on the promise that it can make agentic AI reliable for everyone else. Abbas, Temporal’s CEO who swapped roles with now-CTO Fateev in 2024, decided the company had to prove that on its own first. He calls the effort “AI for Temporal.”
AI adoption as a job requirement
“We are a company of builders, which means it’s not just engineering,” Abbas tells The New Stack. “The entire company needs to re-evaluate how business gets done and how it uses these tools.”
At more than 500 people — 200 of them engineers — that is a lot of re-evaluating. The burden lands on every employee, he says: Examine your own daily workflow, bring some curiosity to the tools, and change how the job gets done. The expectation is not optional, and Abbas was blunt about it to me. Temporal does not mandate a single product, but it does expect people to change how they work.
“If you are still not adopting the right tools to get better, you don’t have a role here at Temporal.”
“If you are still not adopting the right tools to get better, you don’t have a role here at Temporal,” he says. The requirement isn’t to use a specific product, but rather a mandate to adopt the work.
He frames that around growth rather than headcount. Temporal is spending to unlock new work, Abbas says, not to run the same company with fewer people. He does not rank employees on a usage leaderboard because he thinks it creates the wrong incentive. The demand also cuts against the company’s own grain.
Abbas asking Temporal employees to turn experimental without turning reckless, and he says that cultural shift is the harder half of the work.
One of Temporal’s core values is what Abbas calls “reliable as gravity.” Temporal is conservative when it bets on a technical stack. He is asking it to turn experimental without turning reckless, and he says that cultural shift is the harder half of the work.
Temporal
Samar Abbas · Co-founder & CEO
- Claude Code: the default coding tool, adopted on its own after the holidays
- Cursor plus foundation models mostly from OpenAI and Anthropic
- Open-weight models not approved internally; deemed unproven on security and privacy
- Claude Desktop puts app-building in non-technical hands
- Notion + MCP as the shared knowledge base; Slack AI for status
- Built in-house on Temporal: Deputy (security workflow) and model routers
- Vendor costs tracked in Vantage, with hard spending limits
- Finance and engineering review the outliers every two weeks
- No employee token leaderboards, by design
- No absolute dollar figure on the record
- 500+ employees, 200+ engineers, fully remote
- Every function must rebuild its own workflows, not just engineering
- No mandated tool and no usage leaderboard
- Blunt line: adapt or “you don’t have a role here at Temporal”
- Framed as growth, not headcount cuts
- BDR is the most AI-native team; outbound runs as Temporal workloads, hours to minutes
- Revenue roughly doubled this year, by Abbas’s account
- No direct correlation established between AI use and the revenue
- Recruiting prep also compressed from hours to minutes
- Cheap generation collapsed the cost of producing sloppy work
- Reviewers, not authors, became the bottleneck
- Unreviewed AI work reached slide decks and even websites
- Fix is cultural: self-review before you hand off
“It’s not about shipping features faster. It’s about shipping value customers care about.”
Samar Abbas, Co-founder & CEO
On why faster shipping is not the same as value, a gap he says he still cannot measure.
On the engineering side, the tooling is deliberately unmandated. Temporal enables the tier-one options, Cursor and foundation models mostly from OpenAI and Anthropic, and lets engineers settle on what works. Claude Code became the dominant choice on its own after the ‘25 holidays, Abbas says.
What the company has not done is bring open weights inside. Temporal has not broadly approved open-weight models for internal use, which Abbas says remain unproven for its security and privacy requirements. There is no formal model-review process yet; a central AI team vets each new model for security before it is opened up across the company.
Tools beyond engineering
Abbas splits the company into two adoption problems: the technical users and everyone else, and puts the same demand on both. The most surprising adoption is happening away from the engineers. Abbas tells me a nontechnical member of Temporal’s recruiting team used Claude Desktop to build recruiting tools of their own, a job-description builder and an interview-plan builder that turned hours of scattered prep into a running start.
That project is growing into a sourcing agent that pulls and pushes candidate data across Notion and spreadsheets and ranks matches. The knowledge the sourcing agent draws on lives in Notion, wired through MCP into the company’s other systems of record. For a 500-person remote company, that wiring has done more for the non-technical side than any coding tool, letting low-code users reach systems they could not touch before, with whole workflows migrating into Notion pages as a result.
Day-to-day coordination runs through Slack, where Abbas says its AI features have replaced much of his old habit of pinging people for a status update.
Abbas smiles when he tells me the clearest payoff so far is not in engineering at all. Temporal’s business-dev reps, the team that researches prospects and drafts outbound messages, have become the most AI-native group in the company. Work that used to take hours, pulling data from a dozen places and turning it into a first outreach draft, now runs as a custom workload the team builds on Temporal and finishes in minutes. It is the AI-for-Temporal idea: a non-engineering team building on the company’s own infrastructure to turn a slow, manual process into a fast one. What excites Abbas is the loop as much as the saved hours.
Review bottlenecks and AI slop
Like at other organizations, Temporal is seeing AI improve processes but also shift bottlenecks. Point AI at one workload, clear the obvious constraint, and the bottleneck jumps somewhere else. Write more code and review becomes the choke point. It’s the pattern Abbas has become an expert at, and it’s why he distrusts easy wins.
The place it bit was where a reliability company like Temporal would least tolerate it. When code got cheap to produce, reviews got expensive. “AI slop is a real thing,” Abbas says. AI, he argued, has lowered the cost of producing sloppy work so much that reviewers are being flooded with it.
On critical infrastructure, the bar has not moved: Every line still gets read by a person before it’s committed, which makes the reviewer, not the author, the new constraint. It is a squeeze other engineering leaders are feeling, too. Temporal’s fix is cultural. It has made it acceptable to send work back the moment it’s clear the author did not read it themselves first. The slop is not only in code. Abbas has seen unreviewed AI-generated competitor analysis land in slide decks, and similarly sloppy material reach websites.
The AI bill is moving fast, too. AI costs have increased roughly fivefold this year, Abbas says, and most of the increase comes from coding agents. Temporal pulls every vendor charge into Vantage, sets hard ceilings, and every two weeks, finance and engineering meet over the outliers to decide, case by case, whose limits should rise or fall based on the usage patterns. What it will not do is turn that data into a scoreboard.
“A lot of companies created a dashboard of token consumption. We’re not big fans of that, because it creates this race where I need to become the leader in token consumption.”
“A lot of companies created a dashboard of token consumption,” Abbas says. “We’re not big fans of that, because it creates this race where I need to become the leader in token consumption.” Temporal keeps the usage data, he says, but does not expose it as an employee leaderboard or tie it to performance reviews.
Abbas recalled a runaway workflow at an earlier company that ran up $4 million in compute spending on AWS. Temporal’s answer is a value it calls “fly together”: Give people a budget, expect them to spend it like their own money, and catch the runaways with limits instead of shame.
Where the company did automate, it built the automation like software. Temporal’s security team used to file vulnerabilities as tickets and wait for engineers to prioritize them over feature work, which created constant friction between the teams. Now the team runs the whole lifecycle as one long-running durable workflow built on Temporal itself, an internal tool it calls Deputy: Find the flaw, generate the fix, open the PR, merge it, run CI, and roll it out. The security team’s role moved from filing issues to helping ship fixes.
Durable execution for agents
That internal work is also the commercial argument. The problem Temporal spent years on, keeping long-running work alive across failures, is the one many teams building production agents are now encountering.
“These agents are becoming more long-lived, more asynchronous, more mission-critical,” Abbas says. “That is exactly the problem space we’ve been trying to solve with durable execution.”
He describes Temporal’s core as an open foundation model: model-, language-, and cloud-agnostic, with an open-source server companies can run themselves. Inside Temporal, that has taken a solid form. Abbas says the company built an internal platform on Temporal where a non-technical employee can describe an app to Claude Desktop and deploy it in one click.
The guardrails, identity, security, and the MCP connections are wired in, and Temporal’s own model routers keep any single provider from becoming a dependency. The company used its Replay conference in May to make the same case to customers, where it introduced serverless workers, durable streaming, and other features positioned for agent workloads.
For all the speed, Abbas is unusually willing to say he cannot prove it is worth it. Engineering is shipping features 20% to 30% faster with the same-sized team, he says, and he says revenue has roughly doubled since the start of the year, though he is careful to add that he has established no direct correlation between the two.
“It’s not about shipping features faster. It’s about shipping value customers care about.”
He is skeptical of the tidy productivity numbers, that counts of PRs and lines of code, that are supposed to justify the bill. And he thinks the old founder playbook is part of what broke. The advice he got from investors was to do first-principles thinking on product and hire good leaders to run finance, hiring, and go-to-market the standard way. In the AI era, he says, that is backward. The functions everyone used to copy from a playbook are the ones now worth reworking from the start.
Which leaves the number he wants and does not have. “It’s not about shipping features faster. It’s about shipping value customers care about,” Abbas says. And he has yet to see a metric that directly connects the company’s AI use to that outcome.
Temporal knows what the tools cost. It knows they make the company faster. What it still cannot prove is that its customers can absorb the output. For now, that is the bottleneck no agent has cleared.

articles.title: Siri and ChatGPT helped me build a workout plan — one was ‘the better program by some margin’, while the other left me with a ‘one size fits all’ regime
articles.text:
I asked ChatGPT and Siri AI to build me a workout plan — and there was only one winner
Will AI get me fitter or just waste my time?
I’ve been lifting weights at home for a few years now, but recently I’ve found myself stuck in a rut. If anything, my routine has become a humdrum habit, without a clear goal and sense of progression to keep me motivated. Ten exercises, three sets, eight reps, 30 minutes. I’ve run through it so often that I could do it in my sleep.
I’m a true tech lover, so of course I got artificial intelligence (AI) to help me out. Apple has just launched its revamped Siri AI and I’ve been playing around with its early beta edition, so I was curious to know if its new skills extended to solid fitness advice — and if they did, how they held up against the ever-popular ChatGPT.
To find out, I asked each chatbot to dream up a workout routine that could revitalize my fitness habits. After working through both plans and tapping a professional personal trainer for their insights, I was left with the impression that only one of the two workout plans was worth sticking with.
The setup
To start with, I put together a prompt that I then fed into both AIs. The goal was to briefly explain my physical state and outline the kind of workout I was after, noting any constraints such as time and location (I work out at home).
Here’s the prompt I used:
“I am a 36-year-old man in good physical shape who exercises regularly. Create a three-day overall workout plan for me with the goals of hypertrophy and building muscle. The workout will be done in a small home office using dumbbells as the only equipment. It can include calisthenics as well as weighted exercises and should aim to cover different areas of the body. Ensure it lasts no longer than 45 minutes. Explain how often each workout session should be repeated over the course of a week and when rest days should take place, if required.”
I didn’t add any subsequent follow-up messages, as I wanted to know what each AI could come up with given the kind of information that a regular user might provide.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The new challenger: Siri AI
At its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple made a big song and dance of its new Siri AI virtual assistant, a new foundational model based on Google’s Gemini LLM.
When given my workout prompt, Siri AI put together a plan that included a “push” day focusing on my chest, shoulders and triceps; a “pull” day centered on my back, biceps and rear delts; then a final “legs and core” day. It offered a workout schedule and suggested that each session would take around 45 minutes, with three sets of 8-12 reps and a rest of 60-90 seconds between each set.
“Focus on controlled movements and progressive overload by gradually increasing the weight of your dumbbells or the difficulty of your calisthenics,” it advised. Each exercise was accompanied by a short explanation of how to perform it, which was a welcome touch.
Putting Siri’s action plan into practice, it was obvious that my old self-made workout plan wasn't pushing me hard enough, as the first day’s workout left me feeling like I’d worked harder than I had for months. Off to a good start, I thought.
But Siri’s plan came up well short of 45 minutes, with most days’ efforts lasting a mere 25 minutes. And aside from the lack of warm up, there was also no word on how to complement the exercises with targeted nutritional intake. That’s a serious oversight in its workout regimen, especially for beginners.
To help me better understand the plans from both Siri AI and ChatGPT, I asked personal trainer and fitness coach Scott Laidler for his opinion. Speaking of Siri’s effort, Laidler said that it had a few things going for it.
“Siri’s is simple which means there is little to misinterpret,” said Laidler, adding that “the equipment substitutions are sensible for the office environment.”
While Siri recommends upping the weight as you get stronger, it doesn’t say “what to do once this plan hits diminishing returns, which is months away, not years,” according to Laidler. While it sounds like an open-ended plan, “it’s really only built for a defined window,” Laidler warned, which could “lead to frustration unless you knew to come back to the table and ask for a new plan several times per year.”
That’s a problem inherent in the responses from both Siri and ChatGPT.
The class leader: ChatGPT
While Siri AI’s workout plan was concise, ChatGPT was much longer. It explained what the priorities of the workout were and gave some basic advice, such as aiming to finish with one or two reps in reserve as a guidance on how much weight to use. It then listed a weekly schedule before laying out a simple warm up to perform each session.
Each exercise was listed, with varying numbers of sets and reps, followed by a note on which muscle groups were being targeted. Unlike Siri, there was no explanation of how to perform each exercise, which feels like an oversight with potential for injury. That was a clear win for Siri AI.
At the end, ChatGPT included a “progression” section explaining how to push yourself further, a guide on recovery and nutritional intake, then an explanation of “why this split works.” Taken together, it was a detailed workout plan, if a rather verbose one.
According to Laidler, ChatGPT’s plan was “the better program by some margin.” Siri “applies a flat ‘three sets of 8-12’ to every exercise, with each muscle group trained once a week,” Laidler noted. ChatGPT, on the other hand, “hits most muscle groups twice across the week, varies the sets per exercise, includes a warm up, and gives real progression logic. On paper it’s the more sophisticated plan.”
ChatGPT “is closer to what the literature would see as optimal for the stated goal of gaining muscle,” Laidler stated. “Reps in reserve (RIR) offers a way for the user to keep a reasonable distance from failure, which de-risks the plan especially when training alone.”
OpenAI’s LLM has a trick up its sleeve, too: it can analyze your form based on uploaded videos. I asked it to judge my Romanian deadlift form and it gave me an 8.5 out of ten, giving pointers on what I did well and what could be improved. I wouldn’t take this advice over that of a human expert, but compared to Siri AI — which can’t do any of this at all — it’s another point to ChatGPT.
The overall picture
Despite their individual strengths, Laidler warned that neither Siri AI nor ChatGPT had created an optimal workout plan. As he pointed out, “It doesn’t appear that the LLM has asked follow up questions that may have helped customize the plan a little more.”
This highlights a problem with using AI for personal fitness. While a personal trainer would naturally ask these questions straight away, an AI chatbot won’t necessarily propose them unless prompted. Without a more detailed knowledge of your personal situation, you could end up with a sub-par workout routine that’s not well-suited to your circumstances.
So, if you’re going to use AI to sketch out a fitness plan, make sure to add as much detail in your prompt as possible. Ask it to pose follow-up questions to ensure it has as all the information it needs, and come back to it regularly. Don’t just stick to the plan it gives you and repeat it ad infinitum or you’ll end up like I did: languishing, with your progress grinding to a frustrating halt.
Of course, as Laidler pointed out, the problem with doing this — telling the LLM your injury history, what feels like a hard set, your workout preferences, and more — means that “you need to already know what a well-built program looks like to comprehensively prompt for one.” And if that’s the case, do you even need an AI to help you in the first place?
If you do want to go ahead with an AI fitness coach, ChatGPT is a better bet than Siri AI for now, as it includes more varied sets and targets more muscle groups. Neither is perfect, but Apple has plenty of work to do if it wants to match ChatGPT’s take on fitness advice.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Alex Blake has been fooling around with computers since the early 1990s, and since that time he's learned a thing or two about tech. No more than two things, though. That's all his brain can hold. As well as TechRadar, Alex writes for iMore, Digital Trends and Creative Bloq, among others. He was previously commissioning editor at MacFormat magazine. That means he mostly covers the world of Apple and its latest products, but also Windows, computer peripherals, mobile apps, and much more beyond. When not writing, you can find him hiking the English countryside and gaming on his PC.

articles.title: Is this Billboard Hot 100 hit AI slop?
articles.text:
Fenix Flexin is best known as a member of Shoreline Mafia, a rap duo from Los Angeles. But he’s recently found solo success with the track “Rubberz,” which has climbed to number 58 on the Billboard Hot 100. Almost immediately, though, questions were raised about the song’s origins, with many speculating that it was largely, if not entirely, generated by AI. Fenix has denied those accusations, but done little to dispel them.
Is this Billboard Hot 100 hit AI slop?
We can’t be 100 percent sure, but probably.
Is this Billboard Hot 100 hit AI slop?
We can’t be 100 percent sure, but probably.
Part of the suspicion is certainly due to the fact that the song is a dramatic left turn. Fenix has primarily trafficked in trap-influenced West Coast rap. “Rubberz,” on the other hand, is heavily influenced by ‘80s UK synth pop. The vocal melody is clearly influenced by Morrissey, with Fenix even adopting a fake British accent. But artists are allowed to evolve and experiment. That alone doesn’t prove anything.
Perhaps more telling is the simple quality of the recording. Close inspection reveals a number of artifacts and anomalies that are commonly found in AI-generated music. Hi-hats have a certain brittle quality, the chorus vocals sound like a low-bitrate MP3, and reverb tails haphazardly cut off.
Speaking with The Verge, songwriter and co-host of the Switched on Pop podcast, Charlie Harding, highlighted the giveaways. “Ghostly backing vocals duck in and out unexpectedly. The drum reverb is full of unnatural digital artifacting reminiscent of a 64kbps MP3 downloaded off of Napster. Because most generative AI companies have trained their model on low-quality MP3s of unlicensed copyrighted material, we hear audibly degraded instrumentation.”
Feeding the song into an AI music detector doesn’t deliver a smoking gun. I ran the track through five different tools, and they all said that there was between 20 and 30 percent chance that it was AI or at least AI-assisted. But those sorts of tools are not necessarily super reliable and advance much more slowly than music-making models themselves.
Some of the supporting materials, however, have tripped up AI detectors. The single’s cover art and a post celebrating its success were both flagged as being AI-generated with over 97 percent certainty by multiple AI image detectors. Similarly, I fed the lyrics into multiple AI writing detectors and Gemini, which agreed they appeared to be written by AI. Producer and YouTuber Curtiss King dropped the lyrics into Claude, and it also flagged multiple signs that the lyrics appeared to be AI-generated.
The lyrics are the sort of logical near-gibberish that AI often spits out. The rhymes are simple and clean in a way that you wouldn’t expect from someone who is a reasonably accomplished rapper. There are no near rhymes or internal rhymes. Instead, everything sticks to a basic AA, BB format that clearly prioritizes the rhyme scheme over actual meaning or narrative development.
Swipin’ cards and stackin’ chips, I saw you sinkin’ ships
Left me standin’ in the pourin’ rain, now I bought a heavy diamond chain
Who is sinking ships? Are we the sinking ships? No clue, this idea never comes back up. Similarly, the individual lines of the chorus might make sense, but when combined are meaningless.
Bankrolls on the table
Watchin’ local cable
Hatin’ that I’m able
Hatin’ that I’m able
Ignoring the “local cable” bit, which is just awkward (and nearly sent King into a rage spiral), what is Fenix able to do? Why does he hate it? The lyrics raise more questions than they answer.
The way the lines are delivered is also odd. Verse three seemingly ends mid-thought on the line, “Not the jewelry.” Harding noted that it has a “complete lack of flow.” He says that, “No half-competent rapper would ever sing the title line ‘I just let the rubber band snap’ in such an awkward manner. The syncopation is highly unusual, emphasizing all the wrong syllables.” He goes on to explain that, “by smashing so many syllables together, it forces the word the onto the downbeat, instead of the word rubber, forcing all of the subsequent syllables to accent with unnatural syncopation.”
Live “performances” of “Rubberz” haven’t done Fenix any favors. The first couple of in-studio appearances featured the rapper awkwardly lip-syncing. At times it seems like the awkwardness of the flow and the lyrics trip him up, as if he can’t remember his own song. Honestly, he’s not even trying that hard to convince anyone that he’s actually singing.
Things only get worse when Fenix actually does sing. It’s abundantly clear in multiple clips that he is incapable of recreating the vocal range and accent from the recording (and that he doesn’t know the lyrics). In many of the clips of live performances, even when he’s singing, they’re simply playing the original vocals over his. His real vocals are kept extremely low in the mix, and the DJ strategically drops out the backing track briefly in an effort to prove the authenticity of the song, but fails.
Fenix has defended himself, saying the difference between the recorded version and any in-the-flesh performance is down to vocal processing, including AutoTune. However, multiple people, including Harding, King, and Anthony Fantano, have disputed this assertion. King compares AutoTune to spellcheck, and that’s not a bad analogy. While yes, it can be pushed to its limits to create unique robotic textures, it’s designed to clean up errors — it would not extend a performer’s vocal range or introduce an accent, as Fantano points out.
Perhaps the most compelling argument for “Rubberz” being authentic is just how bad it is. Harding says, “I would assume it was written by someone who has never written a song using an ‘80s kids practice keyboard.” If the song was indeed created using generative AI, it was clearly made with an inferior model. “I am concerned that audiences find this song interesting when it is created by one of the lesser generative AI music companies with a terrible model. More sophisticated models have already made big improvements in the audible artifacts and awkwardly sung rhythms.”
Fenix has posted clips of what he says are Pro Tools session files. But that doesn’t actually prove anything. Unless he shares the original recording and project files publicly, it’s likely he’ll never shake the AI allegations. And I don’t see that happening anytime soon.

articles.title: Adobe Campaign Classic CVSS 10.0 Flaw Could Run Code Without User Interaction
articles.text:
Adobe has released security updates to address a maximum-severity security flaw in Campaign Classic (ACC), its enterprise-focused marketing automation platform, that could result in arbitrary code execution.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-48449, carries a severity score of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system.
It has been described as a case of incorrect authorization that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user without requiring any user interaction.
The update also resolves another high-severity flaw (CVE-2026-48448, CVSS score: 8.6) stemming from SQL injection that could pave the way for arbitrary file reads.
"This update addresses critical vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and arbitrary file system read," Adobe said in an advisory. The company noted that it's not aware of any of the flaws being exploited in the wild.
Both shortcomings have been addressed in ACC v7: 7.4.3 build 9398 for Windows and Linux.
Separately, Adobe has also shipped updates to remediate eight critical-rated flaws in Adobe Bridge that could lead to privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution -
- CVE-2026-48395 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An untrusted search path vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
- CVE-2026-48396 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
- CVE-2026-48390 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that leads to privilege escalation
- CVE-2026-48391 (CVSS score: 8.2) - An untrusted search path vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
- CVE-2026-48374 (CVSS score: 7.8) - A path traversal vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
- CVE-2026-48392 (CVSS score: 7.8) - An out-of-bounds write vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
- CVE-2026-48393 (CVSS score: 7.8) - An out-of-bounds write vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
- CVE-2026-48394 (CVSS score: 7.8) - An out-of-bounds write vulnerability that leads to arbitrary code execution
Adobe credited security researcher Kieran ("kaiksi") with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-48390, CVE-2026-48391, CVE-2026-48395, CVE-2026-48396, and CVE-2026-48374, and "yjdfy" for CVE-2026-48392, CVE-2026-48393, and CVE-2026-48394.
Users are advised to apply the latest updates for optimal protection.

articles.title: 10 películas de Prime Video que te sorprenderán
articles.text:
Prime Video es una de las plataformas más curiosas del mundo del streaming. Por un lado y al contrario de gigantes como Netflix y HBO Max, no tiene un catálogo en frecuente renovación. Al contrario, el servicio por suscripción hace una cuidadosa selección de contenido que permite, que su oferta sea cuidadosamente seleccionada. Del terror (en el que marca pauta), hasta estrenos recientes de cartelera. Lo cierto es que Prime Video tiene suficientes opciones para los amantes del cine de hueso rojo o solo los que buscan pasar un buen rato a la distancia de un clic.
Además, sus producciones originales, enfocadas en adaptaciones de éxitos superventas como la saga Culpa mía o el éxito Off Campus, siempre están en renovación. Eso, gracias a que la plataforma está más interesada en captar público fiel que en producir numerosos y frecuentes estrenos. Por lo que buena parte de las colecciones del servicio por suscripción son una combinación entre novedades cinematográficas y sus clásicos más conocidos. Como si eso no fuera suficiente, Prime Video no deja de innovar al explorar en universos de sagas históricas, como el universo de El Señor de los Anillos: Los Anillos de Poder y El joven Sherlock.
Todo lo anterior convierte a Prime Video en la plataforma ideal para los amantes del cine. Pero también los interesados en la experimentación de cine y televisión. Si amas ambas cosas o solo estás en búsqueda de buen contenido para pasar un buen rato, esta lista es para ti. Te dejamos 10 películas de Prime Video que te sorprenderán. Desde un clásico inmediato del cine de terror español, hasta uno de los mayores éxitos del año. Todo para los amantes del mundo del entretenimiento en toda su extensión.
Prueba Amazon Prime Video totalmente gratis durante 30 días y disfruta del catálogo completo de la plataforma sin límites. Solo con darte de alta tendrás acceso instantáneo a las mejores películas y series, además de envíos gratis en Amazon y otras ventajas.
Gaua
Dirigida por Paul Urkijo Alijo, es la película ideal para los amantes del terror. En especial, porque tras explorar la tradición vasca en Errementari e Irati, el director cierra una suerte de trilogía folclórica con un giro sorprendente. Eso, al sumergirse por completo en el oscuro e inquietante imaginario de las deidades nocturnas y las supersticiones rurales del País Vasco. Ambientada en las montañas de Euskadi durante el siglo XVII, indaga en el apogeo de la implacable caza de brujas y la Inquisición. Por lo que la trama sigue a Kattalin (Yune Nogueiras) , una joven que huye de su violento esposo en mitad de la noche.
Al internarse en la negrura del bosque, la protagonista es acechada por una extraña y cambiante presencia mítica conocida como Gaueko. Este, el dios de las tinieblas y regente de la oscuridad. Lo cual abrirá la puerta a un recorrido a través del horror mitológico y mágico de la región. Con una duración de 93 minutos, Gaua destaca por su estructura episódica y un imponente diseño de producción, vestuario y efectos especiales. Lo que le valió nominaciones en los Premios Goya. Una fantástica pieza de época que puedes disfrutar ahora en Prime Video.
Proyecto Salvación
Esta joya de la ciencia contemporánea dirigida por la aclamada dupla de Phil Lord y Christopher Miller es uno de los éxitos de 2026. Y además, una de las joyas de la corona del catálogo de Prime Video. Basada en la novela homónima de Andy Weir (autor de El marciano), la cinta combina ciencia dura, suspenso y humor inteligente. Para eso, la trama sigue a Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling), un profesor de ciencias de secundaria en medio de una situación extraordinaria. Sin saber cómo o el motivo, despierta con amnesia total a bordo de la nave espacial Hail Mary.
Conforme recupera fragmentos de su memoria, Grace descubre que es el único superviviente de una misión desesperada de la que depende el destino de la Tierra. Esta amenazada por unos microorganismos extraterrestres que están extinguiendo la energía del Sol. En medio de la profunda soledad del espacio exterior, el carismático y vulnerable protagonista halla una insólita pero entrañable amistad con Rocky. Este es un alienígena que también busca salvar a su planeta. Lo que llevará a ambos a un viaje extraordinario que te hará llorar y reír, a menudo en la misma escena.
Las ovejas detectives
Esta aventura familiar de 2026, dirigida por Kyle Balda, es ideal si lo que quieres es pasar un rato entrañable y emotivo. Escrita por Craig Mazin (The Last of Us) y basada en la novela de Leonie Swann, la cinta explora la misma premisa del libro. George Hardy (Hugh Jackman) es un noble pastor que cada noche les lee novelas policiacas clásicas a sus ovejas. Todo, asumiendo que no entienden ni una sola palabra. Sin embargo, la rutina de la granja se quiebra drásticamente cuando George aparece muerto en la pradera en circunstancias misteriosas.
Al darse cuenta de que su cuidador fue asesinado, el astuto rebaño decide que los humanos son demasiado torpes para resolver el caso. Por lo que se organiza para encontrar al culpable por su cuenta. Lideradas por la perspicaz Lily, las ovejas deben abandonar por primera vez la comodidad de sus pastos para adentrarse en el complejo mundo humano.
Eso, mientras investigan a una colorida lista de sospechosos locales que codician el testamento del pastor. Con un reparto estelar que en su versión original que incluye a Emma Thompson, Bryan Cranston, Patrick Stewart y Julia Louis-Dreyfus, la cinta sorprende por su profundidad. Eso al explorar temas como la pérdida, el dolor y el duelo de manera elegante y sincera.
He-Man y los Masters del universo
Este es un regalo para nostálgicos que no te puedes perder en Prime Video. Travis Knight trae de regreso al clásico ochentero con una dosis de humor y el más divertido trasfondo de empatía y sensibilidad. Para eso la cinta se enfoca en el príncipe Adam (Nicholas Galitzine), quien vive exiliado en la Tierra tras haber sido separado de sus raíces. Tras quince años lejos de casa, la mística Espada del Poder reaparece para guiarlo de vuelta a su planeta natal, Eternia. El cual encuentra devastado y bajo el cruel y tiránico yugo del malvado Skeletor (Jared Leto).
Para liberar a su gente, Adam debe asumir su responsabilidad heroica y unirse a sus leales aliados. Entre ellos, la guerrera Teela (Camila Mendes) y el valiente mentor Duncan/Man-At-Arms, interpretado por Idris Elba. Juntos emprenden una épica contienda para reclamar los secretos ancestrales del castillo Grayskull. Si amaste la serie animada en tu infancia, esta adaptación encantadora es tu opción ideal.
La boca del diablo
Este thriller de suspenso, terror y supervivencia de 2026 y dirigido por Jeff Wadlow te asombrará. Con un guion coescrito por Aja Gabel y Myung Joh Wesner, la cinta explora el terror acuático y claustrofobia de una manera original. Para eso, la trama sigue a un grupo de cinco amigos universitarios que deciden emprender una excursión guiada a un paisaje enigmático. A saber, un remoto y laberíntico sistema de cuevas subterráneas en la costa de Tailandia. Eso en busca de una última gran aventura antes de asumir las pesadas responsabilidades de la vida adulta.
Sin embargo, la travesía se transforma en una pesadilla letal cuando una tormenta inunda el lugar. Por lo que quedan atrapados en la sofocante oscuridad de las cavernas inundadas. La situación se vuelve verdaderamente desesperada al descubrir que no están solos. Un voraz y sanguinario tiburón toro habita las aguas dulces del complejo y comienza a cazarlos de forma implacable uno a uno.
Mordida
Esta película estadounidense de comedia, suspenso y terror de 2020, escrita y dirigida por Brad Michael Elmore, es una mezcla curiosa. Eso, al ser tanto una historia de crecimiento como una historia de horror. Para eso, la historia sigue a Laurel, una adolescente transgénero interpretada por Nicole Maines, quien decide mudarse a la ciudad de Los Ángeles. Todo, para iniciar una nueva etapa en su vida tras graduarse de la escuela secundaria.
Al poco tiempo de llegar a la caótica metrópoli californiana, Laurel se cruza en el camino de un enigmático y sofisticado grupo de cuatro chicas vampiras. Todas, con una estricta ideología feminista, lideradas por la magnética Duke (Diana Hopper). Tras ser mordida e introducida a este peligroso mundo nocturno, la protagonista debe aprender a controlar sus nuevos instintos sedientos de sangre. Eso, mientras se adapta a las severas e inquebrantables reglas de la manada. Lo que incluye no morder a ninguna mujer y acabar con los hombres que abusan de su poder.
La asistenta
Es uno de los grandes de principios de año que ya puedes disfrutar en Prime Video. Dirigida por el polifacético Paul Feig y escrita por Rebecca Sonnenshine, la cinta es la esperada adaptación cinematográfica de la novela homónima de Freida McFadden. Por lo que la absorbente trama sigue los pasos de Millie Calloway (Sydney Sweeney), una joven con dificultades económicas. También, un pasado turbio que busca desesperadamente una oportunidad para reiniciar su vida.
Su suerte parece cambiar cuando es contratada como empleada interna en la imponente y lujosa mansión de los Winchester. Este, un adinerado matrimonio de la alta sociedad compuesto por el atractivo Andrew (Brandon Sklenar) y la errática e impredecible Nina (Amanda Seyfried). Sin embargo, la rutina doméstica pronto se desmorona al transformarse en un peligroso juego de manipulación, violencia psicológica y oscuros secretos de alcoba. Una combinación que pone en riesgo la cordura y la supervivencia de Millie.
Marty Supreme
Si te perdiste la película de Josh Safdie en su carrera al Oscar esta es la oportunidad de verla. Escrita en colaboración con Ronald Bronstein, la cinta está libremente inspirada en la vida de Marty Reisman. Este, un carismático estafador que se convirtió en una leyenda del tenis de mesa a mediados del siglo pasado. Por lo que la trama sigue a Marty Mauser (Timothée Chalamet), un vendedor de zapatos de Nueva York con una ambición desmesurada. También, con un único objetivo: consagrarse como el mejor jugador de ping-pong del mundo.
El vertiginoso ascenso del protagonista lo arrastra a una espiral frenética de fama, caóticas apuestas clandestinas y lujos desmedidos. Una combinación que amenaza con conducirlo a su propia autodestrucción. Ideal para los amantes de las obras raras y curiosas.
La larga marcha
Esta distopía temprana de Stephen King dirigida por Francis Lawrence y escrita por JT Mollner es una pieza angustiosa que convierte el terror en advertencia. Con una tensión psicológica asfixiante, la trama se ambienta en unos Estados Unidos alternativos y militarizados de la década de 1970. La historia sigue a cincuenta adolescentes elegidos por sorteo para competir en el evento anual más macabro del país. Una caminata televisada sin línea de meta en la que cada participante debe mantener de forma obligatoria un ritmo mínimo de 4.8 kilómetros por hora.
Si un joven reduce la velocidad o se detiene, recibe un aviso. Tras acumular tres advertencias, los soldados que custodian el recorrido lo ejecutan de inmediato en el acto. El último chico que logre quedar en pie ganará una inmensa fortuna en efectivo y la concesión de cualquier deseo que elija para el resto de su vida. El relato se enfoca en Ray Garraty (Cooper Hoffman), quien, a medida que sus fuerzas físicas se agotan, entabla profundos lazos de camaradería, empatía y dolor con sus rivales. Estos, encarnados por David Jonsson, Charlie Plummer y Roman Griffin Davis.
Together
Y una película de terror para finalizar la lista. El director y guionista Michael Shanks indaga en los terrores parasitarios del amor en esta historia retorcida. Para eso, el argumento sigue a Tim y Millie (Dave Franco y Alison Brie), una pareja de muchos años que se encuentra en una profunda crisis emocional.
En un intento desesperado por salvar su relación y alejarse de la rutina, deciden mudarse a una solitaria casa de campo rodeada de naturaleza. Sin embargo, la tensión acumulada entre ambos desata una maldición ligada a una fuerza sobrenatural oculta en una cueva cercana. Con una premisa vagamente inspirada en el mito griego de Hermafrodito y la fuente de Salmacis, es una historia perturbadora que solo encontrarás en Prime Video.

articles.title: Alemanha julga se vazar WhatsApp privado viola lei de dados
articles.text:
Um caso que começou com o fim de uma amizade e mensagens de WhatsApp vazadas pode acabar redefinindo os limites da proteção de dados na União Europeia. O Tribunal Federal de Justiça da Alemanha (a mais alta instância da justiça comum alemã) começou a analisar nesta última quinta-feira (30) o processo, segundo a DW Brasil.
A reclamante trabalhava em um consultório médico e trocou mensagens com uma amiga se queixando do chefe. Três anos depois, quando a amizade terminou, as mensagens chegaram à mulher do chefe — que também trabalhava no consultório. Pouco tempo depois, a funcionária foi demitida.
O que está sendo julgado
A questão central não é a demissão em si, mas se o encaminhamento das mensagens configura violação do Regulamento Geral sobre a Proteção de Dados (RGPD), equivalente europeu da LGPD brasileira.
O RGPD tem uma exceção importante: ele não se aplica ao tratamento de dados pessoais no âmbito da vida privada, sem relação com atividade profissional ou comercial, o que inclui troca de mensagens e redes sociais.
A reclamante argumenta que essa exceção não se aplica ao seu caso. Se vencer, tem direito a indenização de 7,5 mil euros (cerca de R$ 44 mil) além do ressarcimento dos custos com advogados.
Primeira instância condenou, segunda absolveu
O Tribunal Regional de Frankfurt, em primeira instância, condenou a ex-amiga ao pagamento da indenização. O argumento: ela compartilhou deliberadamente as mensagens com alguém próximo ao empregador, alegando querer “proteger” o consultório. Isso configuraria relação com atividade econômica – e, portanto, o RGPD se aplicaria.
O Tribunal Regional Superior de Frankfurt chegou à conclusão oposta. Para a segunda instância, o encaminhamento não tinha relação com atividade profissional da ré. A corte reconheceu que houve interferência ilícita na esfera privada, mas considerou que a violação não foi grave o suficiente para justificar indenização. Uma declaração formal da ré comprometendo-se a não repetir a conduta seria compensação suficiente.
Por que o caso importa além da Alemanha
Segundo Niko Härting, da Associação Alemã dos Advogados, o caso segue duas linhas jurídicas distintas: o direito à proteção de dados e o direito à personalidade.
A questão central para o RGPD é como interpretar a exceção à vida privada: “Deve-se considerar exclusivamente a motivação de quem encaminha os chats ou basta que o destinatário possa utilizá-los em um contexto profissional?”, explicou o advogado à agência DW.
Há pouca jurisprudência sobre o tema. Por isso, os juízes alemães podem consultar o Tribunal de Justiça da União Europeia (TJUE) antes de decidir, já que o TJUE nunca analisou o RGPD no contexto de aplicativos de mensagens. A decisão poderia criar um precedente inédito na Europa.
O TJUE também analisa atualmente outro caso envolvendo privacidade doméstica: uma mãe que processou a filha e o genro por a terem filmado com câmera escondida dentro de casa. Os dois processos não devem ser julgados antes de setembro.
Layse Ventura é editora de SEO no Olhar Digital e mestre pela UFSC.

articles.title: The next big US car trend could be surprisingly small
articles.text:
There’s a micro mobility revolution underway in the USA, spurred on by a rise in popularity of golf carts — could this be a turning point for the country that pioneered gigantic SUVs?
America has opened its doors — and hearts — to tiny transport
America has spent decades building some of the biggest, most powerful and least apologetic vehicles on the planet.
Full-size pickups have dominated the US charts for generations, while SUVs have gradually swallowed up everything from family sedan to station wagon sales.
But something strange is happening at the other end of the automotive spectrum. Golf carts are spreading beyond perfectly manicured golf courses.
Electric bike sales are also booming, with an estimated 2.2 million e-bikes imported to the US in 2025 alone, while various low-speed vehicles (LSVs) are becoming more common on public roads — and manufacturers are suddenly talking seriously about tiny electric cars designed for short hops rather than cross-country road trips.
We reported recently that Fiat has just brought its tiny, sub-$14,000 Topolino EV to the US for the first time, while Swiss company Microlino has gone as far as designing an "anti-pickup truck" specifically for American customers. It's called the Spider, and it's awesome.
Even established automotive and mobility companies are increasingly interested in vehicles that occupy the space between an e-bike and a conventional car.
None of this means Americans are falling out of love with large vehicles. In fact, quite the opposite is true. The EPA's 2025 Automotive Trends Report found SUVs accounted for 60% of all vehicles produced in the US in model year 2024.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
But perhaps that is missing the point. The more interesting question isn't whether a tiny EV can replace a Ford F-150. It's whether Americans are finally realizing that they don't need an F-150, a three-row SUV or even a conventional crossover for every single journey.
Americans love a short journey
For anyone from the UK (or anywhere in Europe, for that matter), America's obsession with hopping in the car for every journey can be baffling.
Granted, this isn't the case for those living in densely packed cities, such as New York or Washington D.C, but in suburban areas it is the norm.
The Washington Post recently reported that roughly 80% of daily US trips are under 10 miles. It's perhaps no surprise, then, that federal rules already recognize low-speed vehicles (LSV) as a distinct category.
Under NHTSA rules, an LSV is a four-wheeled vehicle capable of traveling faster than 20mph but no faster than 25mph, with states and local authorities able to set additional rules around where and how they can be used.
This goes some way toward explaining the recent golf cart boom that has occurred in certain neighborhoods.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the US golf cart market has grown from around $1 billion before the pandemic to roughly $5 billion, with street-legal carts increasingly appearing in suburban communities and being used for everyday trips rather than just on golf courses.
But these aren't the indistinct boxes that ferry players and clubs around the course, as Americans are increasingly turning to "tricked-out" rides that better mirror their personalities.
Modern street-focused carts can come with seat belts, headlights, turn signals and sophisticated equipment, such as navigation technology and booming sound systems.
"Governments, businesses, and facility operators are adopting electric mobility solutions to reduce emissions while improving operational efficiency across campuses, airports, resorts, and residential communities," a recent report by Persistence Market Research reads.
With more sophisticated carts on the way from the likes of Yamaha, Persistence Market Research says the next few years could prove lucrative for established names.
The automotive industry wants in
The arrival of the Fiat Topolino in the US feels almost like a joke at first glance. It has a $13,995 starting price, a 5.4 kWh battery and a top speed of just 19mph in its initial specification. Even after the planned low-speed vehicle conversion, it will only reach 25mph.
But in much of Europe, these are already commonplace and are categorized as light quadricycles.
The segment allows teenagers as young as 14 to hop behind the wheel in some countries, while also offering the benefits of a small footprint for easier parking, lower taxes and often lower insurance costs.
In the US, a Topolino still might seem absurd, but Fiat has a very specific use case in mind. The tiny runaround is designed around low-speed, short-distance mobility, putting it much closer to a neighborhood EV or golf cart alternative than a conventional highway car.
It has already targeted luxury hotel chains, which will be able to personalize the Topolino with bespoke branding and design touches, while upmarket private residential estates could also benefit from the small electric vehicles as a mode of local transport.
The Verge also reported on Micro's introduction of the Spider to the US market last year. The company's founder claims it isn't built for the 5% of trips where you need to haul a lot, but for the 95% of trips where you are alone. He described it as the "antithesis of massive electric pickup trucks."
The small-car comeback is well underway
Kelley Blue Book reported in 2025 that Americans had started choosing smaller vehicles again, noting that compact SUVs became the country's best-selling vehicle type in 2020 and have continued to grow while midsize SUV sales have retreated.
The publication also noted that three compact SUVs — the Toyota RAV4, Tesla Model Y and Honda CR-V — outsold Ram's full-size pickup in 2025.
However, America's love affair with large vehicles clearly isn't over. According to Cox's June 2026 US sales forecast, full-size pickups and midsize SUVs accounted for more than 30% of the market.
But the growth of compact SUVs alongside low-speed vehicles and other micromobility options suggests there is a growing appetite for something smaller than the traditional American default.
Become a TechRadar Insider by simply clicking 'Join Now' at the top of this page. Have a question? Please email membership@techradar.com
The financial argument is becoming harder to ignore, too. Fortune reported that compact SUVs were gaining in popularity because that's "all Americans can afford", reinforcing the idea that smaller vehicles can offer a more accessible entry point for buyers who don't need the extra size.
As a result, a number of automotive newcomers are looking to exploit this newfound interest, with Rivian spin-off Also revealing its innovative, modular e-bike in the TM-B last year, as well as its fully electric TM-Q cargo platform.
Also's President Chris Yu spoke to me about the "pent-up demand" for something more convenient than a car on America's busy streets, with his team investigating how to reduce the pain points of making the switch to an electric bike or quadricycle.
It's not just the US, either, as Honda recently introduced its tiny Super-N EV to the UK, marking the first time it has offered something from Japan's ever-popular kei car segment outside of its domestic market.
With fuel prices spiraling, the cost of vehicles increasing and cities becoming increasingly congested, consumers are looking for innovative ways to get around, and micromobility could be the next big trend that helps keep the world moving.

Leon has been navigating a world where automotive and tech collide for almost 20 years, reporting on everything from in-car entertainment to robotised manufacturing plants. Currently, EVs are the focus of his attentions, but give it a few years and it will be electric vertical take-off and landing craft. Outside of work hours, he can be found tinkering with distinctly analogue motorcycles, because electric motors are no replacement for an old Honda inline four.

articles.title: One California town found Flock's license plate cameras were wrong 71% of the time
articles.text:
In brief: The controversy surrounding Flock cameras primarily centers on privacy and fears of a surveillance state. However, the cloud-based license-plate-reading system's accuracy and effectiveness have also drawn scrutiny. In one particularly egregious case, an internal review uncovered more than 1,000 false positives over two years.
Police in Roseville, California, found that, out of 1,427 incidents in which the town's AI-powered license-plate cameras flagged a vehicle as stolen or used in a felony, the cameras misread the plate in 71% of cases.
Flock, the startup that supplies the cameras to Roseville and approximately 6,000 other communities across the US, attributed the errors to Roseville's atypical camera setup, but as Business Insider reports, the results could expose flaws in an already controversial technology.
Flock's cameras, typically placed on traffic light poles and roadsides, photograph passing vehicles and analyze their characteristics, including license plates, color, make, model, and other details via machine learning. Authorities can search the company's cloud database for vehicles using descriptions to track their movements, which they say has helped solve crimes and find missing persons.
The AI cameras process approximately 20 billion vehicle scans per month and have raised fierce debate across the US. Communities across the country have deactivated their cameras since last year out of concerns about state surveillance, but some towns, including Roseville, are also dealing with the system's blind spots.
There, a police supervisor joked about memorizing one driver's license plate because Flock's cameras misread it at least six times. In each case, the cameras mistook a 9 on his license plate for an 8. This is more likely to happen if a camera takes a blurry image or if the license plate is obscured by a tree or license plate frame.
Ironically, while Flock claims that the errors stem from how Roseville deployed the cameras, the suburb's unique implementation likely also prevented matters from worsening.
To avoid recording drivers' faces, Roseville configured the cameras to only capture vehicles from behind, which Flock says makes them less accurate. However, none of the false positives led to traffic stops, much less arrests, because Roseville officers must verify each report, which is not required in California.
Meanwhile, the LAPD recently let its contract with Flock expire after an internal audit found that 161 innocent people were pulled over in a two-month span. Outdated or inaccurate data from other jurisdictions was cited as a primary cause.
Critics have also pointed out that, despite license-plate reading being their primary function, the AI cameras can also analyze and track people on foot. Police have searched the database for people based on extremely vague descriptions, and numerous officers have been caught using the system to stalk ex-partners.

articles.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day leak racks up millions of views
articles.text:
A bootleg of Spider-Man: Brand New Day was up on X for over seven hours before eventually being pulled. During that time, it reached over 5.9 million accounts and accumulated over 143,000 likes. Other accounts have reposted the leaked film, but none have lasted particularly long, as Disney now seems to be on top of issuing takedown requests.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day leak racks up millions of views
But that didn’t stop it from breaking box office records.
The leak is unlikely to slow down the box office juggernaut, which is already shattering records. It raked in $72 million in previews this week. The previous record holder was Avengers: Endgame, which grossed $60 million during its previews way back in 2019. Endgame went on to set staggering records for opening weekend, grossing over $1.2 billion worldwide and over $350 million in the US. Spider-Man: No Way Home currently holds the number two spot on the all-time US opening weekend list with $260 million.
Brand New Day could potentially usurp Endgame, though it certainly faces an uphill battle. Between previews and opening day, it’s already grossed $168 million, which puts it ahead of Endgame’s $157.4 million. Sony is keeping its estimates somewhat conservative, saying it expects the latest Spider-Man to pull in $325 million.

articles.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma isn't just the best horror movie of the year — it's the best film of 2026 full stop
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
It's possible that never before in the history of cinema has a horror movie been so thoughtful, profound, and moving as Jane Schoenbrun's Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Simply calling it a genre film is doing it a huge disservice — fans will have thoughts and feelings to unpack for years.
Pros
- +Hannah Einbinder is living the LGBT+ dream
- +Gillian Anderson is being the LGBT+ dream
- +Easily Jane Schoenbrun's strongest film to date
- +Stunning 'gothic Wes Anderson' production design
- +Layers upon layers or meaning and messaging
- +You will be moved to tears
- +Incredible soundtrack
- +Shrewdly in control of its time jumping
Cons
- -It ended
Why you can trust TechRadar
Dear Gillian,
When I close my eyes, my version of heaven is you sprinkling rose petals across the bedroom of a deserted log cabin while any song from Sade's Love Deluxe album hums softly in the background. Now, when I open them, I can see exactly that in Teenage Sex and Death in Camp Miasma.
It's an understatement to say that Jane Schoenbrun's third movie was my most anticipated movie of 2026, and that was before I knew anything other than the cast list.
The world's worst-kept secret is that amongst queer women, you're considered to be "lesbian God," thanks to The X-Files, The Fall, Sex Education, and the time you said that the Guess remix featuring Charli XCX and Billie Eilish was your most listened-to song on Spotify in 2024. I'd argue that you've even overtaken Cate Blanchett in that respect.
Add Hannah Einbinder, the woman we've vicariously lived through since season 1 of Hacks, into the mix, and I knew audiences would have something special in their hands. But I really didn't foresee just how profoundly, life-changingly moving the end product would be.
There's a lot of spectacular dynamics at play to make this possible, but I think that the beating heart at the center of it is you. As Billy Presley, the reclusive former 'final girl' of the Camp Miasma horror franchise that director Kris (Einbinder) wants to reboot, we get yet another piece of the never-ending puzzle that is your multi-faceted craft.
Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is more than just a LGBTQIA+ horror movie — it's an epiphany
On the surface, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma should be a straightforward, almost stereotypical horror movie premise. When Kris is asked to direct a reboot of the disgraced Camp Miasma franchise, she visits original movie final girl Billy, who still lives at the summer camp where it was set. Cue an inversion of reality where the pair are literally running for their lives away from the "big bad," Little Death.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
But actually, there are no villains here. This is all just a facade to get you hooked on the true meaty substance of the movie: the subconscious fear in pleasure. For Kris, this manifests in her sexuality, struggling to fully let herself go in the presence of another person. Billy's confident command in leading Kris towards the light (that is, sexual freedom) is... well, satisfying in more ways than one.
Everything is sexy and sensually charged, but nothing is ever gratuitous. It's almost as if Einbinder was inside my own brain before instinctively making her character choices, with every decision Kris makes being the one I'd have chosen myself. She makes no secret of her immediate fascination and hunger for Billy... and isn't that how we react to you as it is?
By now, the internet has worked out that "Little Death" is also how the French describe an orgasm, but I think the significance of the trio's relationship runs so much deeper than just sex. Our spear-wielding villain signifies loneliness, a lack of self-understanding, and a self-imposed inability to give and receive love. Schoenbrun's previous two films, We're All Going to the World's Fair and I Saw the TV Glow, explore these phenomena beautifully, but by God, has she achieved an all-timer here.
Across the board, everything is elevated, from the movie's scale and production design to its soundtrack and grasp on moving through time. Aesthetically, we land directly between fantasy and reality, with hand-drawn backgrounds often representing Billy's romanticized version of her Camp Miasma truth. Kris is the conduit between the two, but when she finally gives herself over to Little Death, she exists in a blissful, ever-moving fantasy that I would now do anything to claim for myself.
The act of pleasure in itself can look like just about anything, and you all innately understand that. As Little Death sits in his video palace with a completely different understanding of what the Camp Miasma movies can mean, I find myself wanting to be brave for them all. I want to scream, cry, and grasp hold of joy for them. I want to meet myself at my most basic, primal level.
But back to you, Gillian
But enough of this... let's get back to you. Armed with a Dolly Parton-esque accent, a bucket of fried chicken and a lifetime's resistance against assimilating back into the real world, Billy Presley is the new-age horror hero I didn't know I needed.
Kris might be the bridge between the world of Camp Miasma and real life, but Billy is our guide between harbored shame and unrelenting freedom. She understands life in a way that most of us never do, perhaps because we've long left our sense of whimsy and suspension of belief behind. To her, Little Death is as real as you and I, and I'm starting to believe the same thing.
You've simultaneously made Billy into the most mysteriously sexy woman alive and an adult posing as the frightened, unsure teenage girl who never grew up after the release of the franchise's first movie. She's a beacon of never-ending wisdom, yet has absolutely no understanding of how the outside world works. She's the embodiment of how people can be everything and nothing all at once, and that is a pleasure to behold in itself.
If she could trap me under that picturesque starlit sky while little on the porch of the cabin she now calls home, I'd never move. If she reached for my hand to stay close through a woodland storm of bloodied clothes and peach skies, I'd walk forever. Kris felt the same way, and now she gets the blissful, blood-soaked happy ever after with her lover that the LGBT+-friendly side of cinema has only let us have a handful of times. The one so many of us long for.
Kris gets it. Einbinder and Schoenbrun get it. And now, I get it too. Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma isn't just a movie, but a life-altering experience, and you made sure of that. In a twisted sort of way, sex, death, and the life we live in between the two have never been more appealing.
Thank you for keeping us grounded in our own pleasure, whatever it looks like.
Yours,
Jasmine Valentine
